```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 80)
library(cytokineR)
library(data.table)
```

The goal of pre-processing a multi-batch, multi-cohort cytokine study is one
dataset in which samples from every plate, kit lot and cohort can be compared,
ready for analyses that may not even be planned yet. Choosing the pipeline
carries three risks:

1. **Under-correction.** Plate, batch or cohort effects remain and show up as
   false findings, or hide real ones.
2. **Over-correction.** The correction removes biology along with the
   technical variation, for example when plates or cohorts differ for real
   reasons.
3. **Overfitting the choice.** Trying many pipelines and keeping the best one
   rewards whichever pipeline happens to fit the noise in this particular
   dataset.

This vignette goes through a workflow that addresses all three:

- candidate steps;
- an unseen test set;
- criteria for harmonisation and biology;
- the choice, made on the training samples only;
- a check of that choice on the test samples;
- the final dataset, exported with a report of how it was made.

## 1. Candidate steps

Write down the steps you are considering, in processing order. Steps that
are not in question go in `fixed`; the others are switched on and off in
every combination (2^K pipelines for K optional steps).

```{r}
steps <- list(
  log2   = pipe_transform("log2"),
  beads  = pipe_custom(function(x) flag_beads(x, 35), label = "beads"),
  median = pipe_normalize("median", within = "time"),
  ctrl   = pipe_normalize("anchor", anchors = "ctrl_low", scope = "batch"),
  bridge = pipe_correct_batch("bridge")
)
```

Any step can be optional, including calibration (`pipe_calibrate("shared")`)
and imputation (`pipe_impute("rank_tobit")`). A transform such as
`pipe_transform("mob")`, switched on after `log2`, replaces log2 FI with
multiples of blank, so it also works as an on/off choice. Keep K small: each
extra step doubles the number of pipelines and the number of chances to
overfit.

## 2. An unseen test set

```{r}
test <- split_samples(cyto_example, prop = 0.4, by = "subject",
                      strata = "batch")
length(test)
```

This takes 40% of the subjects, with all their samples, stratified by batch
so that every batch is represented on both sides. With cohorts, stratify by
cohort too (`strata` takes one column, so combine them if needed). Subjects
whose samples serve as bridges between batches stay in training, so batch
correction keeps its anchors.

During selection every row of a test sample gets `use_for_fit = FALSE`.
Plate centring, batch correction and imputation are fitted without these
samples and then applied to them as if they were new data. The test samples
also play no part in choosing the pipeline. Their scores are therefore an
honest estimate of how the chosen pipeline does on data it has not seen.
(Methods that ignore `use_for_fit`, here `combat`, cannot keep that
promise.)

## 3. Criteria: harmonised, but with the biology kept

Each criterion is computed per pipeline, separately on the training and on
the test samples:

```{r}
criteria <- list(
  # residual batch and plate effects among study samples, within time point
  batch   = sample_metric(metric_plate_effect, by = "batch", within = "time"),
  plate   = sample_metric(metric_plate_effect, by = "plate", within = "time"),
  # known biology that must survive: change over time within subject
  biology = sample_metric(metric_bio, ~ time, adjust = ~ subject),
  # agreement of a control that no step may fit on, across batches
  control = default_metrics()$reliability_batch
)
```

* `batch` and `plate` are adjusted partial R² values: the share of variation
  explained by batch or plate after accounting for time point. Lower is
  better, and 0 means no detectable effect. Accounting for the strata
  (`within`) matters: if one cohort is sicker than another, a cohort effect
  is partly real and should not be "corrected" away.
* `biology` guards against over-correction. A pipeline that flattens
  everything would win on `batch` and lose here. Use a variable whose
  effect you trust, such as time, a treatment, or a known group difference.
  Don't use the effect your study is about.
* `control` uses material held out from all fitting (`holdout` below).
  Because it does not depend on which samples are in training or test, it
  gives the same value for both; it helps the choice but is not an
  independent check.
* Any model can be a criterion as well: `model_statistic()` wraps `lm()`,
  `glm()`, `lmer()` and so on (see `vignette("waterfall-lattice")`).

## 4. Choose on the training samples

```{r}
sel <- select_pipeline(cyto_example, steps, criteria, test = test,
                       fixed = "log2", holdout = "ctrl_high",
                       resolution = 0.01)
sel
```

Pipelines are ranked on each criterion, and the mean rank decides.
`resolution = 0.01` makes differences smaller than 0.01 count as ties, and
ties go to the pipeline with fewer steps. Without it, the third decimal of a
batch R² can decide the choice, which is chasing noise. A simpler pipeline
that is as good as a complex one is also less likely to fail on the next
batch. Use `weights` if some criteria matter more than others.

```{r, include = FALSE}
ch <- sel$scores[selected == TRUE]
none <- sel$scores[pipeline == "none"]
```

The chosen pipeline is **`r sel$selected`**. Without any correction, batch
explains `r round(none$batch_test, 3)` of the variation among the unseen
test samples (adjusted partial R²). With the chosen pipeline it explains
`r round(ch$batch_test, 3)`. For plate the figures are
`r round(none$plate_test, 3)` and `r round(ch$plate_test, 3)`, and the time
effect within subjects stays at `r round(ch$biology_test, 3)`.

## 5. Check the choice on the unseen samples

```{r}
plot(sel)
```

Each panel is one criterion, and each point is one pipeline. Points near
the dashed line score the same on unseen samples as in training. The choice
generalises when the chosen pipeline (orange) lies close to that line on
every criterion. The blue point, the best pipeline on test, is there to
show how much better the choice could have been. Choosing by it would
overfit the test set.

Every criterion also has a lattice that shows what each step contributes,
here the residual batch effect on the test samples:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot(sel$lattices[["batch::test"]], "contributions")
```

### Will it work for a new cohort?

A stricter check holds out a whole batch, or a whole cohort, as if it
arrived later:

```{r}
new_batch <- split_samples(cyto_example, by = "batch", values = "2")
criteria_new <- criteria
# a single held-out batch has no batch effect of its own: compare it with
# the training samples instead
criteria_new$batch <- sample_metric(metric_plate_effect, by = "batch",
                                    within = "time", pool_test = TRUE)
criteria_new$plate <- NULL
sel_new <- select_pipeline(cyto_example, steps, criteria_new,
                           test = new_batch, fixed = "log2",
                           holdout = "ctrl_high", resolution = 0.01)
sel_new$scores[, .(pipeline, batch_test = round(batch_test, 3),
                   biology_train = round(biology_train, 3),
                   biology_test = round(biology_test, 3))][1:8]
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
bt <- sel_new$scores
med <- bt[pipeline == "median"]
```

Here the study samples of batch 2 are unseen, so on its plates sample-based
median centring can only be fitted on the few bridging samples. The time
effect measured in batch 2 then drops to `r round(med$biology_test, 3)`
with median centring alone, compared with `r round(bt[pipeline == "bridge",
biology_test], 3)` with bridge correction alone. Steps that are fitted on
material present on every plate (controls, bridges) carry over to a new
cohort better than steps that need its samples.

## 6. Produce, export and document the dataset

```{r}
final <- finalise_pipeline(cyto_example, sel)
final
```

`finalise_pipeline()` runs the chosen pipeline on the raw data. With
`refit = TRUE` (the default) all samples, test samples included, are used for
the final estimates: the test set has done its job, and more data give more
stable corrections. With `refit = FALSE` the test samples stay out of the
fits, exactly as when they were scored. How the pipeline was chosen is
stored in the object (`final$meta$selection`).

```{r}
processing_report(final)
```

The report is ready for a methods section. `export_dataset()` writes
everything a later analysis needs:

```{r}
out <- export_dataset(final, file.path(tempdir(), "study"), name = "study")
basename(out)
```

* `study_wide.csv`: one row per sample, one column per analyte: the values
  to analyse;
* `study_long.csv`: every measurement with censoring, limits, imputation and
  QC flags;
* `study_report.md`: the processing report;
* `study.rds`: the `cyto` object with the full log and stored estimates
  (`cyto_steps()`, `cyto_fit()`).

When a new batch or cohort arrives, combine it with the raw data
(`cyto_bind()`) and run `finalise_pipeline(raw_all, sel$pipeline)`. Batch
correction is anchored to the reference batch, so the scale stays the same.
Steps that pool information across batches can still shift earlier values
slightly, so re-export the whole dataset rather than appending to the old
files, and keep the old report for comparison.

## Checklist

* Decide the candidate steps and criteria **before** looking at the
  results, and keep the number of optional steps small.
* Set aside a test set of whole subjects, stratified by batch and cohort.
  Keep bridging samples and anchor material in training.
* Use at least one harmonisation criterion and one biology criterion, and
  account for real differences between groups (`within`).
* Choose on the training samples only, with a `resolution` that ignores
  differences too small to matter.
* Report the test scores of the chosen pipeline, not the best test scores.
* Hold out a whole batch or cohort if the dataset will grow.
* Export the dataset with its processing report.
